prompt: Thesis statement: Euthanasia should be banned. Generate a paragraph agreeing or disagreeing this thesis statement.
reference_answer: I disagree with the statement that euthanasia should be banned. Euthanasia allows terminally ill patients to end their suffering with dignity when no medical treatment can relieve their pain. Banning it forces people to endure prolonged agony, which can be physically and emotionally devastating for both patients and their families. With strict legal safeguards, informed consent, and medical supervision, euthanasia can be carried out ethically and compassionately. Respecting an individuals autonomy over their own life and death decisions is a fundamental ethical principle, and denying this right can be seen as inhumane. Therefore, rather than banning euthanasia, societies should focus on regulated, ethical implementation.

prompt: Thesis statement: Animal testing is good for humankind. Generate a paragraph agreeing or disagreeing this thesis statement.
reference_answer: I disagree with the statement that animal testing is good for humankind. While it has historically contributed to some medical advancements, animal testing raises serious ethical concerns because it causes pain, suffering, and often death to sentient creatures. Moreover, results from animal experiments do not always translate reliably to humans due to biological differences, leading to ineffective or harmful outcomes. Advances in alternative research methods, such as cell cultures, organ-on-a-chip technology, and computer modeling, offer more ethical and often more accurate ways to study diseases and develop treatments. Therefore, relying on animal testing is both morally problematic and scientifically unnecessary.

prompt: Briefly summarize (max 15 words): Kubernetes provides a way to declaratively define how your application should run. You give it a blueprint (a YAML file) stating: I want three instances of my web app, each connected to a database, using this much CPU and memory. Kubernetes then makes it happen across the available machines in the cluster. It pulls your container images from a registry and gets them running. 2. Scaling: If your application becomes more popular and needs more capacity, you can tell Kubernetes to scale up (e.g., from three instances to ten). Kubernetes will automatically start new container instances across the cluster to handle the increased load. When traffic decreases, you can scale down to save resources. 3. Management (The Orchestration Magic): This is where Kubernetes truly shines. It continuously monitors the state of your applications and ensures it matches your blueprint. Self-Healing: If a container crashes, Kubernetes automatically restarts it. If an entire machine fails, Kubernetes will reschedule the containers that were on it onto other healthy machines. Service Discovery and Load Balancing: Kubernetes can give each set of applications a stable IP address and DNS name and distribute network traffic between them, so other applications can find them easily. Rolling Updates and Rollbacks: You can deploy a new version of your application seamlessly. Kubernetes will gradually replace old containers with new ones, ensuring zero downtime. If something goes wrong with the new version, it can instantly roll back to the previous version. Storage Orchestration: It can automatically mount storage systems (like local storage or cloud storage from AWS or Google Cloud) to your containers.
reference_answer: Kubernetes automates deployment, scaling, self-healing, load balancing, updates, and storage for containerized applications.
